key_insight: Vision-language models do not simply follow what they see; their internal components can be traced as either amplifying visual evidence or letting prior knowledge override it when the two conflict. The paper shows this behavior has a causal, component-level basis across multiple model families.
problem_solved: The paper addresses the challenge of understanding how multimodal models resolve conflicts between visual input and memorized world knowledge, moving beyond behavioral descriptions to identify which internal parts cause the model to trust vision versus prior knowledge.
method: Uses activation patching at three levels of granularity: residual stream, attention heads, and MLP sublayers.
Combines patching with component ablation to test which parts of the model are causally responsible for perception-knowledge conflict resolution.
Performs mechanistic analysis across three vision-language model families to compare whether visual grounding or prior knowledge dominates under conflict.
impact: This work gives practitioners a clearer map of where multimodal errors come from inside the model, which can help with debugging, interpretability, and safer deployment. It also informs strategies for improving robustness when models face misleading or ambiguous visual inputs.

paper_title: Vision-Default, Prior-Override: Causal Mechanisms of Perception-Knowledge Conflict in Vision-Language Models
paper_authors: Niclas Lietzow, Danielle Bitterman, Carsten Eickhoff, William Rudman, Michal Golovanevsky
